corrections.source_says: The 10 named chatbots are Microsoft Copilot (creative mode), ChatGPT-3.5, Bard, Llama2, Pi, Character Assistant, Perplexity AI, Copy AI, Claude (Claude-instant via Poe.com), and Vicuna (Vicuna-13B). They performed the task individually, in writing and in English, using standardized initial/repeat/transition prompts. Repeated prompting continued until the human median number of uses was reached or surpassed, the chatbot refused, or it exactly repeated earlier uses. corrections.source_says: The AUT objects were fork, balloon, and key. Human dyads brainstormed aloud in German, with 3 minutes per object; their responses were transcribed. Chatbots answered in written English under the response-count stopping rule rather than the same time limit. The divergent_test classification is confirmed.

corrections.source_says: Replace the unknown generic outcome with the reported AUT dimensions: fluency (number of valid uses), originality/novelty (rarity of use categories), flexibility (number of distinct use categories per dyad/chatbot), elaboration (detail), and the overall sum of all four dimensions. Human scorers coded the responses independently and resolved differences by consensus; counts use category_count and rated scores use human_raters, with no stated expert qualifications. Repeated or incomprehensible uses were removed. Each comparison answers question = none because it compares AI-generated with human-generated output. The group-exclusive category analysis is also reported separately on p. 5.
corrections.quote: Two scorers first scored the uses individually, and then compared and discussed scoring dif- ferences until a consensus was reached.

confirmed: The paper contains one AI-versus-human output comparison; design_class = ai_vs_human and context_class = ai_vs_human are correct (workshop PDF, p. 1, Abstract and Section 1; p. 3, Section 4.2).

No people received generative-AI assistance in the reported study; the comparative experiment with AI-supported human dyads is explicitly proposed as future work (workshop PDF, p. 3, Section 4.2; p. 6, Section 6).

The compared groups are student dyads and 10 independently tested chatbots; 40 students constitute 20 dyads, and the 10 systems are not people (workshop PDF, p. 3, Sections 4.2-4.3; p. 4, Table 1; p. 5, Table 3).
The task is the Alternate Uses Test, so divergent_test is correct; population = students is also correct (workshop PDF, p. 3, Sections 4.1-4.3).
The human responses were produced without AI, and the outcomes compare separate human and AI output; question = none and comparison_type = ai_vs_human are correct (workshop PDF, p. 3, Section 4.2).
Participant-level randomization and recruitment totals are not given; n_randomized should remain null (workshop PDF, p. 3, Sections 4.2-4.3).
The outcome scores are based on actual responses, with independent coding by two scorers followed by consensus, and are aggregated per dyad/chatbot (workshop PDF, pp. 3-4, Section 4.5).
The source reports 783 valid human uses and 395 valid chatbot uses, and states 1178 uses in total; these counts describe outputs rather than people (workshop PDF, p. 3, Section 4.4; p. 6, Section 6).
The study is not a synthesis; the blank synthesis fields and null pooled-study/effect counts remain appropriate (workshop PDF, pp. 3-6, Sections 4-6).
All eight PDF pages were read, including the references on pp. 7-8; the PDF contains no appendix and does not identify supplementary results (workshop PDF, pp. 1-8).
summary: The retrieved eight-page TREW 2024 paper confirms the ai_vs_human context classification and contains no randomized study of people receiving AI assistance. The form needs source metadata, the analyzed count of 40 students in 20 dyads (below 50), dyad-level scoring and reported results, and the link to the pre-study summarized in c032.
